blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Decode a brief — form, audience, purpose, role and focus — and write to fulfil it, whatever form it names.

blocks.heading: The brief
blocks.text: A brief is the specification a piece of writing must fulfil: its form, audience, purpose, role and any focus the prompt adds. The brief is not a suggestion — every word of it is part of the task, and the fifteen marks of Paper 2 Question 1(a) are for a piece of no more than 400 words whose vocabulary, style and structure fit it. Read the brief twice before writing a word, and write its five parts down where they can be checked.

blocks.heading: Decoding the brief
blocks.text: Decoding runs in order. The form: what kind of text — speech, email, report, blog, story opening? The audience: who reads it — the hall, the cousin, the officials? The purpose: what must it do — persuade, describe, inform, entertain? The role: who is speaking — the head learner, the visitor, the club secretary? The focus: what extra thing does the prompt demand — "introduce both sides", "create a sense of unease"? Five answers, written down, and the piece is planned before it is written.

blocks.heading: Form is not purpose
blocks.text: A task’s form and its purpose are separate: a speech that informs and a speech that persuades are different speeches, and the difference shows in every choice — the informing speech signposts and explains; the persuading speech presses and asks. Writing the form without its purpose produces the right container with nothing inside: a report laid out faultlessly that recommends nothing, a speech addressed to the hall that asks the hall for nothing.

blocks.heading: Worked example: decoding done properly
blocks.text: A prompt sets: "Write a speech for a school debate, as the first speaker for the motion, introducing both sides of the question of school uniform." The decode: form, a speech; audience, the hall of learners and teachers; purpose, to open the debate persuasively; role, first speaker for the motion; focus, introduce both sides — the one requirement a learner most often drops. The piece that argues one side only has missed the focus in the prompt’s last four words, and its fifteen marks are marked as a poorer fit to the task even though every sentence might be well written.

blocks.heading: Three ways to miss the brief
blocks.text: The first error is writing in a different form from the one set — a story where a description was asked for — which misses the task whatever the quality of the writing, because the form is part of the specification. The second is ignoring the role or the occasion: a debate speech that never opens the debate, a report written by nobody in particular, leaves the brief half-decoded. The third is missing the focus sentence: the piece persuades without reasons when the prompt asked for reasons, or describes without the sense of calm the prompt named. Each error is checked the same way: reread the brief, name its five parts, and test the piece against all five.
